title: sports-betting
text:
sports-betting is a set of tools for building, testing and using sports betting models. You can use it from Python, from the command line, or through an AI agent.
There are two main parts. A dataloader downloads the data and shapes it for modelling. You build it from a statistics source and an odds source, so you always know where your data came from:
from sportsbet.dataloaders import DataLoader
from sportsbet.sources import FootballDataOdds, FootballDataStats

dataloader = DataLoader(
    param_grid={'league': ['England'], 'division': [1], 'year': [2023, 2024]},
    stats=FootballDataStats(),
    odds=FootballDataOdds(),
)
X, Y, O = dataloader.extract_train_data(odds_type='market_maximum')
print(X.shape)
(760, 29)
That’s two seasons of the English top division: 760 matches, each with 29 columns.
The second part is the bettor. It wraps any scikit-learn estimator, backtests a strategy on the data, and predicts the value bets of upcoming matches.
The library can also place a bet for you. Be careful with this, because it spends real money. Some bookmakers have an API, and for the rest an agent drives their website on your account, which breaches most bookmakers’ terms of service and puts your account at risk.
Install it with pip install sports-betting.

title: scikit-ai
text:
scikit-ai provides task-oriented components for text, images, audio and video that follow the scikit-learn estimator API.
Components are named by what goes in and what comes out, like ImageClassifier, AudioSegmenter or TextToVideoGenerator, so the name tells you what each one does. Since they are estimators, they fit into Pipeline, GridSearchCV and the rest of scikit-learn.
Here is a text classifier that learns from a few labelled examples:
from skai.classification import TextClassifier

X = ['I loved this movie.', 'The product broke after a day.', 'Great service!', 'Never again.']
y = ['positive', 'negative', 'positive', 'negative']

classifier = TextClassifier(k_shot=2, random_state=0, backend='dummy').fit(X, y)
print(classifier.predict(['What a wonderful day.']))
['negative']
The backend parameter decides what actually runs the task. It can be local open-source models through Hugging Face, the OpenAI API, other providers through LiteLLM, or models hosted on Replicate. The code stays the same.
I used the dummy backend above, which is why it calls a wonderful day negative. It comes with the base install and needs no models or credentials, but its outputs are placeholders, so swap it for a real one to get real predictions.
Note that fit doesn’t train a model unless you ask for fine-tuning. A classifier, for example, keeps your samples as examples for the model to work from.
Install it with pip install scikit-ai, and add an extra such as scikit-ai[hf] or scikit-ai[openai] for the backend you want.

title: imbalanced-learn-extra
text:
imbalanced-learn-extra extends imbalanced-learn with oversamplers it leaves out, usually because they are newer or less cited. It has two main parts.
The first is a general interface for clustering-based oversampling. SMOTE and its variants only look at the imbalance between classes, but a class can also be imbalanced within itself. Clustering the data first helps with that. You can combine any clusterer with any oversampler, so here is k-means with SMOTE:
from collections import Counter
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
from imblearn_extra.clover.over_sampling import ClusterOverSampler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
print(Counter(y.tolist()))

oversampler = ClusterOverSampler(
    oversampler=SMOTE(random_state=0), clusterer=KMeans(n_clusters=10, random_state=0, n_init=10)
)
_, y_resampled = oversampler.fit_resample(X, y)
print(Counter(y_resampled.tolist()))
Counter({1: 357, 0: 212})
Counter({0: 357, 1: 357})
The second is Geometric SMOTE. SMOTE creates new samples by interpolating on a line between existing ones. Geometric SMOTE expands that area, and it works as a drop-in replacement:
from collections import Counter
from imblearn_extra.gsmote import GeometricSMOTE
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
_, y_resampled = GeometricSMOTE(random_state=0).fit_resample(X, y)
print(Counter(y_resampled.tolist()))
Counter({0: 357, 1: 357})
Both follow the imbalanced-learn API, so they fit into scikit-learn style pipelines. Install it with pip install imbalanced-learn-extra.

title: agentorg
text:
agentorg is a framework for generating multi-agent organisations from one Python file, spec.py. It’s still early and isn’t on PyPI yet, so install it from GitHub:
pip install git+https://github.com/georgedouzas/agentorg.git
agentorg --help
Usage: agentorg [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

  Agentorg: Generate runnable multi-agent organisations.

Options:
  --version  Show the version and exit.
  --help     Show this message and exit.

Commands:
  new     Interview the user to assemble an agentorg spec.py.
  render  Render a project from a specification file.
  ui      Run the browser-based master interview UI.
agentorg new starts an interview with a master agent, which fills in the spec for you. There is also agentorg ui if you prefer a browser. The interview moves through five stages: discover, configure, build, refine and handoff. Each stage’s agent only has the tools for that stage, so the discovery agent can’t set your organisation’s identity by accident.
agentorg render then turns the spec into a project. By default that’s the full thing, with a backend and a React dashboard. You can also render just the frontend, backend or AI layer.
The master agent uses Agno, but your own agents, teams and workflows don’t have to. In the spec, each one can be anything runnable, like a plain async function.

title: copier-modern-python
text:
copier-modern-python is a Copier template for modern Python projects. It asks you a few questions and generates a project with its tooling already configured.
copier copy "gh:georgedouzas/copier-modern-python.git" my-project
ls -A my-project
With the default answers, you get this:
.copier-answers.yml
.editorconfig
.github
.gitignore
.pre-commit-config.yaml
CHANGELOG.md
CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
CONTRIBUTING.md
LICENSE
README.md
docs
noxfile.py
openspec
properdocs.yml
pyproject.toml
renovate.json
src
tests
The questions cover your package manager (PDM or uv), your Git provider, the license, the Python versions you support, and the project layout: a library, a command line tool, machine learning, data engineering or a service. You can also add a Dockerfile, and choose a spec-driven workflow with OpenSpec, Spec Kit or neither.
Nox runs the tasks, including tests across Python versions, formatting, checks and building the docs.
Copier also remembers your answers, so copier update applies later template changes while keeping your own settings.

title: mathpix-mcp
text:
mathpix-mcp is a Model Context Protocol server for Mathpix OCR. It lets an LLM or agent turn images and PDF, DOCX or PPTX documents into LaTeX and Markdown.
It’s written in Ruby, so you need Ruby 3.2 or newer and your own Mathpix credentials:
gem install mathpix-mcp
export MATHPIX_APP_ID=your-app-id
export MATHPIX_APP_KEY=your-app-key
mathpix-mcp
That runs it over stdio. There is also a mathpix-mcp-http executable for Streamable HTTP, with bearer-token authentication. An agent that connects gets these tools:
convert_image_tool
convert_document_tool
convert_strokes_tool
batch_convert_tool
check_document_status_tool
search_results_tool
get_usage_tool
get_account_info_tool
list_formats_tool
OCR output is always written to a file and never returned inline. The tool sends back a path, a short preview and some metadata. A long PDF can produce a lot of text, and this stops it from overflowing the model’s context.

title: scikit-complexity
text:
scikit-complexity is a Python library to create and simulate complex systems. You describe a model in a few lines, and it works out the mathematics, picks a solver and runs the simulation.
It handles differential equations, stochastic processes, discrete maps, cellular automata, agents, networks and fields through one interface. There are two ways to use it.
The first is the model catalog in skcomplex.models. Pick a ready-made model and run it:
from skcomplex.models import describe, run

print(describe('lotka_volterra').description)

trajectory = run('lotka_volterra').trajectory_
print(trajectory.names)
Prey and predators whose populations oscillate through predation.
['prey.n', 'predators.n', 'growth.r', 'predation.a', 'predation.b', 'death.d']
The second is skcomplex.core, for your own models. A model is made of elements, which carry state, and interactions, which change that state through laws. Here is the same kind of predator and prey system, written from scratch:
from skcomplex.core.elements import CompartmentElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import RateInteraction
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation
system = System(
    elements=[CompartmentElement('rabbits', n=40), CompartmentElement('foxes', n=9)],
    interactions=[
        RateInteraction('r', target='rabbits', state='n', sources=['foxes'],
            rate=lambda s: 1.1 * s.target.n - 0.4 * s.target.n * s.sources[0].n),
        RateInteraction('f', target='foxes', state='n', sources=['rabbits'],
            rate=lambda s: 0.1 * s.target.n * s.sources[0].n - 0.4 * s.target.n),
    ],
)
trajectory = Simulation(system, dt=0.05).check().prepare().run(until=30).trajectory_
print(round(float(trajectory.values('rabbits.n').max())))
53
That is the highest rabbit population reached during the run.
You don’t have to state what kind of model you are building. You write the laws, and the library decides whether it is an ODE, an SDE or a jump process. Add a RerunObserver and the run streams live to the Rerun viewer, where you can watch it while changing its parameters.
The catalog is listed in the gallery, from Game of Life to Schelling segregation. Its models use the same public classes you do, so each one doubles as an example for your own.
Install it with pip install scikit-complexity. It runs on Linux and on macOS with Apple silicon, and on Windows through WSL.

title: Veriphy
text:
Veriphy is a set of agent skills and a Lean 4 toolkit for machine-verified math and physics, from a single theorem to a whole paper.
It treats both SageMath and the agent as untrusted. Sage finds what is expensive to find, like coefficients or closed forms. A script turns that into a Lean tactic block, and the Lean kernel accepts it or rejects it. A Sage bug or an agent’s mistake can waste your time, but it can’t produce a false theorem. The finished proofs are plain Lean and build with mathlib alone, so CI never needs Sage.
You give it a statement in plain language:
/veriphy:prove the partition function Z(β) = 2cosh(βh) satisfies ∂²(log Z)/∂β² = h²/cosh²(βh)
The agent states the claim in Lean. Lean can’t tell whether that statement means what you said, so the agent translates it back to English to compare, then tests it in Sage. Only then does it try to prove it. You get a proof, a counterexample, or a report of what blocked it.
For a draft or a paper, /veriphy:research goes through every claim and writes a verification appendix. A theorem is only as strong as what it rests on, so one that relies on a lemma Sage merely tested gets a lower level, and the report names that lemma. There is one limit: nothing checks that a claim in your prose and its Lean statement say the same thing. You have to confirm that yourself.
You’ll need SageMath and elan. The README has the install steps.
